newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn nears deal on deficit cuts, but doubts remain.
newsitem.headline: Bonn nears deal on deficit cuts, but doubts remain.

text.p: Germany's embattled coalition government moved closer to agreement on Thursday on how to plug budget holes without raising taxes, but it was still far from certain the plan could pass both houses of parliament.

Leaders in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and the junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats (FPD), said they were near a deal to close corporate tax loopholes that would help negate a projected 30 billion mark ($17.4 billion) deficit for 1998.

The coalition has teetered on the brink of collapse in recent weeks because the liberal FDP has adamantly refused to consider tax increases proposed by the Christian Democrats to fill gaps in the 1997 and 1998 budgets.

Eager to qualify for Europe's single currency, Kohl's government is desperately trying to push the 1997 deficit to levels below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- the threshold for entry into economic and monetary union (EMU).

The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) forecast on Thursday that public deficits in Germany, France and Italy would all miss the target, hitting 3.2 percent of GDP this year.

Coalition sources said they could close the 1998 deficit by raising about eight billion marks through the introduction of limits on the losses corporations could carry forward into future years to set off against profits.
Another 25 billion marks could be raised by selling part of the government's 74 percent holding in Deutsche Telekom -- 10 billion marks this year and 15 billion in 1998.
Beyond that, a further seven billion marks could be obtained for the 1998 budget through privatisations and other measures.
"We would then have enough without having to raise taxes," one coalition source told Reuters.
It was uncertain how the Social Democrats (SPD), who can veto parts of the legislation through their majority in the upper house of parliament, would react to the plan.

But one SPD leader denounced the proposal and said Finance Minister Theo Waigel was about to make another huge mistake by selling Telekom shares before the original target date of 2000. She said he had failed to learn from his humiliating retreat from an earlier plan, dubbed "Goldfinger", to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves.

"It is hard to imagine how a government can make so many mistakes," said the SPD's finance expert Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier. "After operation Goldfinger, the next mistake is going to be Operation Telekom. They'll get less money now for Telekom than if they were to wait until the year 2000."
The drive to qualify for the euro has left the 14-year-old coalition badly splintered.

"There is a lack of clarity at the moment and we have to end that," said Peter Mueller, leader of the CDU in the state of Saar. "Proposals are shooting off in every which direction. The voters won't accept this chaos."

Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, a leading figure in the pro-business FDP, was quoted in the Handelsblatt newspaper as saying Bonn plans to sell 7.3 million tonnes of oil from its strategic reserves to help relieve strained government finances.

Rexrodt was quoted as saying the oil stocks were worth some 1.4 billion marks. Offering petroleum for sale could raise around 500 million marks a year in both 1997 and 1998, but Rexrodt said the sale would not have an impact on the world oil market.
FDP budget expert Juergen Koppelin said there was room for cuts in the defence budget.

In an interview in the Neue Osnabruecker Zeitung daily, Koppelin said he believed Defence Minister Volker Ruehe could reduce the number of conscripts each year by 20,000 and the number of reserve officers by 1,000. That would save 710 million marks per year.
Koppelin criticised Ruehe for dumping unpaid bills worth two billion marks from 1996 into the 1997 budget year and warned the FDP would not tolerate such "budgetary tricks" any more.
He also repeated his doubts about whether Germany could afford the four-nation Eurofighter project in the light of the current budget troubles.
($ = 1.722 German Marks)
